name: Langkawi Sky Bridge
label: Langkawi Sky Bridge
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/201795658: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Langkawi Sky Bridge' (19 m across).
notes: Curved pedestrian cable-stayed bridge high on Mount Mat Cincang.

text.description: Langkawi Sky Bridge is a curved walkway hanging from a single tall pylon on the top of Gunung Mat Cincang, 660 metres above sea level. It is 125 metres long and was designed with its bend so that the view changes as you walk along it. That is what makes it good for phone photos: every few steps the railings, the cables and the valley line up differently. The bridge opened to the public in 2005, closed in 2012 for upgrading, and reopened in 2015 (partially in February, with the SkyGlide finished in December 2015). It is a pedestrian bridge only, and it is fairly narrow, so you will often be sharing the deck with other visitors. There is a small triangular platform at each end where you can stop without blocking anyone. Use these for your longer pauses. The sloping pylon and its fan of cables make a strong shape against the sky, so try one shot that includes them. Keep another for the green hillsides and the drop below the railings. Hold the phone with both hands, keep strap and fingers clear of the lens, and take a few frames of each view because people keep moving through. Because you reach the bridge from the cable car's Top Station, check the official site before you go for current access, tickets and any weather closures.
text.geographic_location: The bridge is on the summit of Gunung Mat Cincang, on Pulau Langkawi, the main island of the Langkawi archipelago in Kedah, Malaysia. It links two hilltops next to the top of the Langkawi Cable Car.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops apply here. Take the Langkawi Cable Car up to the Top Station. From there the SkyGlide inclined lift takes you down to the bridge in about two minutes. Alternatively, you can follow a steep mountain track on foot, which takes roughly 10 to 20 minutes and is less secure underfoot. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the curve of the deck, the pylon and the cables in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for pictures of people on the bridge, and the telephoto (2x to 5x, depending on your phone) for faraway hills and sea.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Take your first photos here, then walk to either end platform for a view back along the curve.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and use the railing as a leading line that curves away from you. Put the pylon and cables on one third of the frame and leave the valley on the other. Crouch slightly for a low shot of the deck, and keep the phone clear of the mesh at the sides so it does not catch the wire.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the railing or a person, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out. Skip panorama mode, because the bridge and other visitors move and it will stitch badly. Wipe the lens first, as mist or fingerprints cause haze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go early in the day if you can, when the bridge is likely to be quieter and the summit clearer. Cloud or mist can come in later and hide the view, so check the weather before you go up.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed attraction reached by cable car, so check the official site before you go for current access, tickets and weather closures.
claims_not_in_sources: Early in the day the bridge is likely to be quieter and the summit clearer.
Cloud or mist often builds up on the summit later in the day and can hide the view.
Panorama mode usually stitches badly on a busy, moving bridge.
The bridge is often busy with other visitors.

name: Pantai Cenang
label: Pantai Cenang
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pantai Chenang Plaza' (3 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Food Truck Centre Feeder 3 Pantai Chenang' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OSM N11707308069 (SMJ Money Exchange & Remittance (Pantai Chenang Langkawi) (SMJ Teratai)): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
Pantai Cenang is one of Langkawi's best-known stretches of white sand, and the easiest place to start is the central beach entrance, a public square called Pantai Chenang Plaza. A rainbow-coloured Pantai Chenang sign stands here, and behind it you can see the beach and the Andaman Sea. That makes a ready-made foreground for a sunset picture: the sign tells people where they are, and the sea and sky fill the rest of the frame.

Guides name this square as the classic sunset backdrop, so expect company. One blog says people gather opposite Cenang Mall to watch the sun go down, and it is busiest at weekends. If you want a clear view of the sign, arrive well before the sun is low and take your pictures first, then relax and enjoy the colours.

Face west toward the sea. Stand a few steps back from the sign so it sits low in the frame, with the horizon about a third of the way up. If the crowd is thick, move along the sand and shoot at a slight angle rather than waiting for a gap. If you would rather be away from the busy sign area, Casa del Mar is described as a less crowded section of the beach, with the boardwalk and sea in view.
text.geographic_location: Pantai Cenang is on Langkawi and looks out toward the Andaman Sea. The photo spot is the central beach entrance; one blog places it opposite Cenang Mall.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed for this part of Langkawi, so arrange your own transport from wherever you are staying on the island. Head for Pantai Chenang Plaza, the central beach entrance. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the sign with the beach and sunset behind it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sky and sea, or to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the sun low over the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pantai Chenang Plaza (central beach entrance, facing west toward the sea). The rainbow-coloured Pantai Chenang sign in the foreground with the beach and the sunset over the Andaman Sea behind it. From here the rainbow-coloured sign should be in the foreground, with the beach and the sunset over the Andaman Sea behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, keeping it level. Place the sign low in the frame as a foreground. If the square is crowded, take a few steps along the sand and angle the shot slightly. A less crowded part of the beach near Casa del Mar has the boardwalk and sea in view, if you want to get away from the sign area.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright sky near the sun, then slide the exposure down a little so the colours stay rich and the sky does not wash out. The sign may then look darker, which suits a silhouette. For a properly lit sign, take a second shot earlier, tapping on the sign to focus. Take a Live Photo too if you want a little movement from the waves.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset. One blog gives roughly 7.15–7.40pm as the usual window, but check the sunset time for your date and arrive early to claim a spot.

text.access_note: This is an open public square and beach with no charge mentioned in the guides; check the official site before you go if you have any doubts.

name: Kilim Karst Geoforest Park
label: Kilim Geoforest
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kilim Geoforest Park sign cliff' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N5309678721 (Entrance Kilim Geoforest Park): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Mangrove and limestone karst reached by boat tours.

text.description:
Kilim Karst Geoforest Park is a stretch of limestone cliffs, rivers, mangroves and open sea on Langkawi. This spot is the park's best-known photo: the white park name painted on a limestone cliff, with turquoise water below. Guides treat it as the standard picture of the park, and boats usually stop here on the way back, so it works as the classic postcard view. You take it from the boat, looking at the sea-facing side of the cliff, with the boat's edge and the open water in the foreground. That foreground gives the picture some depth and shows people at home where you were.

Most of the park is reached by boat, usually from the Kilim jetty (Jeti Sungai Kilim), so you see this view from the water rather than from land. Boats may not stop at exactly the same point on every trip, so don't rely on one perfect angle. Take a few frames while the boat is slowing or holding still, and keep your arms steady against your body.

If you have time, two other stops are worth a photo. Gorilla Mountain is a limestone outcrop whose shape suggests a gorilla's head and shoulders, framed by the river and green trees. Santuari Bakau has mangrove roots, birds and river views from a raised wooden walkway, which suits a closer, quieter shot of the forest. The far end of that walkway has no protective barrier, so take care there.
text.geographic_location: In the Kilim area of Langkawi, where the limestone cliffs meet the sea. Most visitors start from the Kilim jetty.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or tram stops near here. Tour boats usually leave from the Kilim jetty (Jeti Sungai Kilim), which you can look up on the map. From there, the cliff with the park name is reached by tour boat, not on foot. The boat usually stops at the sign on the way back, but the exact stop can vary, so ask your tour operator. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the cliff, the water and a bit of the boat all fit in. If the boat stops further away, try telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to bring the painted name closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of sea and sky, and keep the cliff away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. You take this photo from the tour boat, facing the sea-facing side of the limestone cliff with the park name. The white park name is painted on the rock above the turquoise water, with the boat and open sea in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the painted name on the upper third, with water filling the lower part and a corner of the boat for scale. Keep the horizon level, because the boat will be moving. For a second shot, turn to the quieter side of the same stop and include open sea. Gorilla Mountain is a good alternative if the boat does not stop at the sign.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the cliff to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white lettering and bright sky do not wash out. Turn on Live Photos or motion if your phone has it, so you can choose the sharpest frame once the boat has settled. Wipe the lens first, as sea spray leaves smears.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Boats usually stop here on the return leg, so this is when you are most likely to get the shot. Try to take it when the sun is not directly in front of the cliff, and ask your tour operator when the stop is likely.

text.access_note: Most of the park is reached by boat tour, usually from the Kilim jetty, so check the official site or your tour operator before you go for access, tour details and tide-dependent stops.
claims_not_in_sources: Shooting with the sun directly in front of the cliff can wash out the lettering and sky.
Sea spray can smear a phone lens.
The boat may be moving or rocking, so keeping the horizon level and the arms steady helps.

text.description: Underwater World Langkawi is rank 4 on this map. It is an aquarium, so most of your photos will be of what lives behind the glass rather than of the building. The main challenge is the light. Tanks are usually dim, and the glass picks up reflections from your own clothes and from lights behind you. Move close to the glass, hold the top of your phone almost against it, and the reflections mostly disappear. Fish move quickly, so take several frames and keep the best one. Wide views of a big tank work well in ultra-wide. Single animals suit the default lens (1x) or a little zoom. Outside, a quick shot of the entrance makes a nice record of the visit. Please keep the flash off. It reflects in the glass and can bother the animals. Rules on photography, bags and tripods inside can differ, and entry is likely to be ticketed, so check the official site before you go. I have no further history, size or date details to share for this spot.
text.geographic_location: Underwater World Langkawi is on the island of Langkawi, Malaysia. Use the map coordinates to find its exact position.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so use the map and follow the phone icon to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the attraction itself, so there is no extra walk and no bearing to follow once you are there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) for large tanks and for the entrance, and the default lens (1x) for most animal shots. Try 2x or more if your phone has it, for a single fish, but expect softer pictures in dim light.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Inside, stand close to the glass, square-on, rather than at an angle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the horizon of the water or the tank edge on a grid line. Put your phone against or very near the glass to cut reflections. Leave some space in front of a moving animal so it has room to swim into the frame. For an outside shot, include the whole entrance and a little of the surroundings.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the animal to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the bright water washes out. If the tank is very dark, let night mode work and hold still. Try Live Photos or motion for fish, then choose the sharpest frame. Keep the flash off.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Go when you have time to wait for a good moment. Fewer people around means you can reach the glass more easily, so a quieter time of day is usually easier. Outside, daylight gives the best entrance shot.

text.access_note: This is likely a ticketed attraction, so check the official site before you go for entry and photography rules.

name: Tanjung Rhu
label: Tanjung Rhu
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jalan Tanjung Rhu' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Jalan Tanjung Rhu nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OSM R4013309 (Tanjung Rhu Public Beach): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: White sand beach with limestone islets and mangroves.

text.description: Tanjung Rhu is a beach on Langkawi where limestone islands rise out of calm, shallow water just offshore. The scene works well on a phone because it has clear layers: sand or road in the foreground, the sea in the middle, then the rocky islets and the sky. The photo spot here is not the sand itself but Jalan Tanjung Rhu, the tree-lined road that leads down to the beachfront. It is lined with casuarina (Rhu) trees, and their rows make natural leading lines that draw the eye towards the beach. The trunks and branches frame the view on both sides, which suits portraits of friends or family with the trees behind and around them. It is also quieter than the beach. Once you have your road shots, walk down to the beach for the other classic views. At sunset the sky colours up behind the limestone islands. When the sand is wet, it can carry reflections of the sea and sky out towards the islets. The sandbar can only be reached at certain states of the tide, so plan around that and keep an eye on the water. Conditions can change, and one visitor reported jellyfish and poor visibility during extreme tides. Parking near the beach may be charged and access points may be restricted, so check locally before you go.
text.geographic_location: Tanjung Rhu is on Langkawi, Malaysia. The road leads down to the beachfront.
text.directions_text: There are no rail or tram stops listed near this spot, so check local transport options before you go. Parking may be charged, so check locally. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the road and trees. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole tunnel of trees and the beach at the end. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from the beach to pull the limestone islets closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Tanjung Rhu (the tree-lined road leading down to the beachfront). A road lined with casuarina trees that leads the eye toward the beach, useful for portraits with the trees as foreground and background. Look along Jalan Tanjung Rhu, the tree-lined road leading down to the beachfront, where the casuarina trees line both sides and lead the eye towards the beach.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the road in the centre, so the trees on each side converge. For portraits, put your subject in the middle of the road with the trees as foreground and background. If you want a different view, the beach itself (Pantai Tanjung Rhu) shows the limestone islands rising from calm water, or a wide strip of wet sand leading out to the islets.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on your subject or the far end of the road, then lower the exposure slider slightly so the bright sky doesn't wash out. Use portrait mode for people in front of the trees. Try a Live Photo on the beach to catch moving water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunset is a good choice for the beach, when the sky colours up behind the limestone islands. Check the tide before you go if you want the wet sand or the sandbar.

text.access_note: The road and beach appear to be public space, but access points and parking may be restricted or charged, so check locally before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Wet sand at lower tides gives better reflections of the sea and sky.

name: Langkawi Cable Car
label: Cable Car
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Eagle's Nest Skywalk' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Eagle's Nest SkyWalk' (way/1561897178): middle (38 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/604085204: the OpenStreetMap point 'Langkawi SkyCab'.
notes: Gondola ride up Mount Mat Cincang with sweeping island views.

text.description:
Langkawi Cable Car, also called Langkawi SkyCab, is a gondola lift that climbs from Oriental Village at Teluk Burau up Gunung Machinchang, on the west side of the island. The full line is 2.2 km long and the ride to the top takes around 15 minutes. It opened to the public in 2002 and was officially opened in 2003. The slope between the base and the middle station is about 42°, said to be one of the steepest of its kind in the world. The gondolas run roughly 70 metres above the forest canopy, so the line makes a strong diagonal across a rainforest shot.

A good vantage point for gondola shots is the middle station platform, at about 650 m above sea level. Stand on the platform near the SkyBistro cafe and look back down the slope. With a little zoom you can frame a gondola climbing through the trees, with Oriental Village far below. It also works well with a friend posed on the viewing deck and the gondola rising behind them. The platform is described as a free viewing area, but you need a ride ticket to reach it, so check the official site before you go.

If you want a second angle, Oriental Village gives a ground-level view of the lake and bridge with the line rising towards the mountain. The top station decks look over the islands and the Andaman Sea. Haze or cloud can reduce the view from the top, and the cars stop in strong winds.
text.geographic_location: On the west coast of the main island of Langkawi, in Teluk Burau, just north of Telaga Harbour at Pantai Kok. The base station is inside Oriental Village at the foot of the Mat Chincang range.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stops serve this spot. It is about 30 minutes' drive from Kuah town and about 15 minutes from Langkawi International Airport, which lies to the south-east. Head for Oriental Village, where the base station is, then ride the gondolas to the middle station, where the Eagle's Nest Skywalk platform is. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull a single gondola in tight against the rainforest. Use the default lens (1x) for the platform, the slope and the village far below. Try ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole ridge and sky, because the gondolas will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (middle station platform, near the SkyBistro cafe). From the middle station, a telephoto shot can frame the ascending gondolas against the rainforest, with the Oriental Village base far below. On the middle station platform near the SkyBistro cafe. From here you can look down the slope and frame the gondolas climbing from the base station, with Oriental Village far below. A friend can pose on the middle-station viewing deck while you shoot from the cafe side, with a gondola behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the gondola line along a diagonal, with the forest filling the lower part of the frame. Wait for a gondola to enter the shot instead of chasing one. If you want a different view, Oriental Village gives a ground-level shot of the lake and bridge with the line rising over the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gondola to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its detail. Take a few frames or a Live Photo as the gondola passes, then pick the sharpest one.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a clear day, and probably earlier in the day, as haze or cloud can cut visibility. Check the weather first, since the cable car stops in strong winds and for bad weather.

text.access_note: The platforms are described as free to enjoy, but you need a cable car ticket to reach them, so check the official site before you go.

name: Telaga Tujuh
label: Telaga Tujuh
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Telaga Tujuh' (4 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W663589959 (Jalan Telaga Tujuh): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Cascading waterfall and natural rock pools.

text.description:
Telaga Tujuh is a waterfall in the rainforest on Langkawi. Its lower falls are a single tall drop of about 91 m, ending in a rock pool. The lower falls are also the easiest part to reach, so you can get the full height of the cascade in view.

The picture here is the water framed by dark green forest on both sides, with the pool in the foreground. On a phone, that gives you a strong vertical shot, or a wide shot that includes the rocks and the trees. Water that is flowing well looks best, but conditions change with the weather and the season, so what you see may differ from other people's photos.

A second place to shoot from is the wooden bridge over the stream, Jambatan Telaga Tujuh. From there you get a wider view of the waterfall and the rainforest canopy around it.

Keep safety in mind. Rocks near water can be slippery, and sudden surges of water can come down after heavy rain, so move away if the stream rises. Do not go near the edge of the upper pools to get a photo. Drones are subject to local rules. Wipe your lens before shooting, because spray and humidity quickly leave it hazy.
text.geographic_location: Telaga Tujuh is on Jalan Telaga Tujuh, in the rainforest on Langkawi.
text.directions_text: There are no rail or tram stops here, so check local transport options for getting to Telaga Tujuh on Jalan Telaga Tujuh. The base of the lower falls is the easiest part of the falls to reach. Once you are at the pool, you are at the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full height of the cascade, the trees and the pool in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the falls. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the water falling against the dark rock.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the full height of the lower cascade is framed by rainforest, with the rock pool at its base in front of you. Stay on firm, dry ground and well back from any drop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn your phone upright and switch on the gridlines. Put the waterfall on a vertical line and the pool along the bottom third. Include some rock or leaves in the foreground to give a sense of scale. For a wider view, hold the phone sideways and use 0.5x. For a different view, try Jambatan Telaga Tujuh, the wooden bridge over the stream, which gives a wide view of the waterfall and the forest canopy.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the water to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white water keeps its detail. For the silky-water look, try a Live Photo or motion effect if your phone has one, and brace your elbows against your body or a rock to keep the phone steady. Wipe the lens first, as spray quickly leaves a haze.

text.access_note: Entrance fees are unclear, so check with LADA or the tourism board before you go.

name: Eagle Square
label: Eagle Square
pin_note: Position from OSM W1257682539 (Eagle Square): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Giant eagle statue on the Kuah waterfront.

text.description:
Eagle Square is a photo spot on the Langkawi map, and the name suggests an eagle statue as the main subject. If the statue is visible on arrival, step back as far as is comfortable so you can fit the whole thing into a phone frame. If the sky is visible behind it, you may get a clean, simple background.

The simplest approach is to start wide and then move in. Use the default lens (1x) for a straightforward shot of the eagle with some of its surroundings. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want to include more sky or the ground around it. Keep your phone level, as tilting upwards makes the statue lean. Gridlines help with this. If you want a detail of the wings or head, use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) rather than walking right underneath.

The statue may be brighter than the sky behind it, so tap the eagle to focus and slide the exposure down a little if the sky starts to wash out. If you want a souvenir picture of yourselves, ask a passer-by to take it from a few steps back so the eagle and your group both fit. Take a few frames with and without people in them, in case other people are in the shot.
text.directions_text: Walk east to reach it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the eagle and its surroundings. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more sky and open space, and telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for close-ups of the wings and head.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (walkway and main entrance in front of the eagle statue). The full 12 m eagle with the square's star-shaped base in the foreground and Kuah Bay and boats behind it. Walk east for about 6-7 minutes on foot, then pick a spot a good few steps back from the statue so it fits in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the phone level so the statue does not lean. Leave a little sky above the eagle's head. For a second picture, move round to a different side and use the ultra-wide (0.5x) from a low position to make the statue look taller.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the eagle to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks too bright. Take a few extra frames, as someone may walk through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually more comfortable and gives softer light. Midday sun can make the statue look harsh.

text.access_note: This looks like an open public space, but check the official site before you go in case any areas are restricted.

Sky may be visible behind the statue.
Early morning and late afternoon give softer, more comfortable light than midday.
It is an open public space, though some areas may be restricted.

notes: Secluded rainforest-backed bay in the northwest.

text.description:
Datai Bay is a curved bay on Langkawi, with forested foothills on one side and a small island, Pulau Anak Datai, sitting in the water ahead. That mix of curve, hills and island makes it a good scene for a phone: the shape of the bay is clear even in a quick snap, and the island gives your eye somewhere to land.

The sand is largely reserved for resort guests, and guides say access is limited to guests or people with permission. You can still get the view from Jalan Datai, the narrow forest road that branches off past The Andaman resort and leads down towards the beach. It is the public viewpoint, and the easiest way to see the whole bay without going into the resort.

Start wide to take in the whole curve, then move in on the island. If you are on Jalan Datai, keep to the edge of the road and stay aware of passing vehicles, because it is narrow. If you would like a quieter coastal view as well, Pantai Pasir Tengkorak is a calmer stretch of clear, white-sand shoreline on the bay's northern side. It is a free public spot, but check its position on the map before you set out.

Bring a little patience: the trees can frame the bay nicely if you step a metre or two left or right until the gaps line up.
text.geographic_location: Datai Bay is on Langkawi, reached by Jalan Datai, the forest road that branches off past The Andaman resort.
text.directions_text: No train or tram stations are listed nearby. Head towards The Andaman resort and take Jalan Datai, the narrow forest road that branches off past it and runs down towards the beach; this is the public viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole curve of the bay and the foothills. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out Pulau Anak Datai.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Jalan Datai (the narrow forest road that branches off past The Andaman resort and leads down toward the beach). A wide view of the curved bay, with the mountain foothills on one side and the small island Pulau Anak Datai in the water ahead. From here you see a wide view of the curved bay, with the mountain foothills on one side and the small island Pulau Anak Datai in the water ahead. Jalan Datai is the public viewpoint; if you use it, stay at the edge of the narrow road.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the island on one of the third-lines, with the curve of the shoreline leading towards it. Use the trees along the road as a natural frame at the edge of the picture. Pantai Pasir Tengkorak, on the bay's northern side, makes a good alternative for a coastline shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the island to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky and sea keep their colour. Take a panorama if you want the full sweep of the bay, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the water.

text.access_note: The beach is a private resort beach and the sand is largely reserved for resort guests, so enjoy the view from the public road and check the official site before you go.

label: Gunung Mat Cincang
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pantai Kok' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Pantai Kok' (pois).

notes: Ancient rainforest mountain on the west of the island.

text.description: Mount Mat Cincang (Gunung Mat Cincang) is the big forested ridge that rises behind the beaches on the north-west side of Langkawi. It is a big, layered backdrop for a phone photo. The best-known frame is from Pantai Kok. You stand at the waterline and look inland, with turquoise water and sand in the foreground and the forested peaks rising behind. A travel guide describes this as the classic view of the mountain and suggests golden hour. The mountain is far too big to fit in a close-up, so the beach is what gives the picture its scale. Let the water, a strip of sand or a figure walking along the shore take up the lower third, and leave the peaks to fill the upper part. If the sky is hazy, the ridge will look flatter, so a few minutes of waiting for a clearer patch can help. Pantai Burau gives a different version of the view, showing the bay with the mountains forming a backdrop across the water. The summit hike is strenuous, and this photo does not need it. Everything here is taken from beach level.
text.geographic_location: Mount Mat Cincang is on the north-west side of Langkawi island, and the guide recommends Pantai Kok for the view of it. The mountain rises inland, behind the beach.
text.directions_text: No Underground, train or tram stops are listed near this spot. Pantai Kok is reached by taxi or car, as the guides note, so ask the driver for the beach by name. Once you are on the sand, walk to the waterline and turn to face inland. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole scene of beach, water and mountain. Try telephoto (2x-3x) to bring the peaks closer and make them look taller. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, such as ripples or footprints, and keep the horizon level.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Pantai Kok (waterline, facing inland toward the mountain). The forested peaks of Gunung Mat Cincang rising behind the beach and turquoise water in the foreground. For the classic view, the guide recommends Pantai Kok: stand at the waterline and face inland toward the mountain. From there the photo shows the forested peaks of Gunung Mat Cincang rising behind the beach, with turquoise water in the foreground. It is not the place where the photo was taken, so do not treat it as being on the Pantai Kok waterline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon, or the water's edge, on the lower line so the peaks take up the top two thirds. Keep some water or wet sand in the bottom of the frame to give it depth. If you want a different view, Pantai Burau shows the bay with the mountains behind the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the mountain to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky looks washed out. This keeps the forest colours rich and the sky from turning white. Wipe the lens before you shoot, as salt spray and sunscreen leave a haze.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Golden hour, according to the beach guide. The low light brings out the colour of the water and the texture of the forested slopes.

text.access_note: Pantai Kok is an open public beach, said to be open 24 hours with free entrance, but check locally before you go; the cable car and summit are paid and separate from this beach view.

label: Pantai Tengah

notes: Quieter beach just south of Cenang.

text.description:
Pantai Tengah is a beach on Langkawi's west coast, and it is a good place to take holiday photographs. One guide describes it as about 700 m long. The sand curves gently, so you can photograph long, sweeping lines of shore, with palms or casuarina trees framing the view and the Andaman Sea beyond.

The most useful viewpoint is at the northern end of the beach. Here a scattering of coastal rock formations gives you a slightly higher position. From there you look down the coastline, with the beach curving below you and the sea and offshore islands spread out ahead. It is a quieter alternative to standing on the open sand. Only one guide mentions these rocks, so check they are still easy to climb when you arrive, and take care on them.

Two other pictures are worth having. At dusk the shoreline faces west, so you can catch the sun setting over the sea with trees on the sand as a frame. Near the island-hopping pier you can photograph colourful local fishing and island-hopping boats moored with green hillsides behind them. Check the exact pier on the map, as its name here is only a descriptive label.

Keep your phone lens clean from sea spray, and keep your shots simple. Put the curve of the beach on one side of the frame and leave plenty of sea and sky.
text.geographic_location: Pantai Tengah is on the west coast of Langkawi's main island, along Jalan Pantai Tengah.
text.directions_text: There are no stations or stops listed for this spot, so navigate to Pantai Tengah using the map. The phone icon on the map marks the spot on the beach. For a higher view, one guide suggests walking to the northern end of the beach, where there are coastal rock formations. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the beach curving away below you. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more sea and sky, and use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out offshore islands or boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For a higher view, walk to the northern end of Pantai Tengah, where one guide reports coastal rock formations. From there you look down the coastline and out over the sea and offshore islands, with the beach curving below you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the curve of the shoreline along one third of the frame, with the sea and islands filling the rest. Keep the horizon level. For a different picture, the sunset shoreline with trees framing the sand works well, and so do the moored boats near the island-hopping pier.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or islands to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour. Try panorama mode along the curve of the beach, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk is a good time, when the sun sets over the Andaman Sea on the west-facing shoreline.

text.access_note: Pantai Tengah is a public beach, but the rocks at the northern end may be uneven, so look at the ground before climbing and check they are still easy to climb.
claims_not_in_sources: Coastal rocks can be uneven or slippery, so care is needed when climbing them.
Sea spray can leave marks on a phone lens, so it is worth wiping it clean.

text.description: Makam Mahsuri is the tomb of Mahsuri, the young woman at the centre of one of Langkawi's best-known legends. According to local tradition she was executed after being accused of adultery, and her name is also used for a secondary school in Kuah. The tomb is the natural postcard frame here: a flat white marble slab set in a lawn and garden, with a traditional Malay house and trees around it. The white stone against the green lawn gives a clean, simple picture, and the traditional Malay house adds a sense of place without needing a wide view. A quieter, looser frame is also possible, with shade trees and benches and the tomb compound in the background. For a phone, you can take a straight-on shot of the slab, a wider garden scene and a tighter detail, with the house in the surroundings. Keep the slab level using gridlines, and wait a moment for other visitors to step out of the frame. Photography is generally allowed outdoors, but some indoor areas, such as the audio-visual room, are off-limits to cameras. The compound has an entry fee, so check the official site before you go for current details.
text.geographic_location: Makam Mahsuri stands on Jalan Makam Mahsuri on Langkawi, in Kedah, about 12 to 13 km from the town of Kuah (check on the day).
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so start from Kuah, the main town, and head to Jalan Makam Mahsuri. Guides put the tomb at about 12 to 13 km from Kuah (check on the day). Once inside the compound, head for the tomb garden and stand in front of the white marble tomb. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the white tomb slab with the Malay house behind it. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole lawn and garden, and to 2x or more for the house details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here the flat white slab sits in the lawn, with the traditional Malay house and trees around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the slab up with them so it sits level, with the house and trees filling the background. For a quieter alternative, step back towards the shade trees and benches and take a looser shot with the tomb compound behind. Keep other visitors out of the frame by waiting a moment.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white marble to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the stone keeps its detail and does not turn into a plain white patch.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No fixed time is needed; gentler light in the morning or later afternoon should suit the white marble best, and fewer visitors make the lawn easier to photograph.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed compound with an entry fee, and some indoor areas do not allow cameras, so check the official site before you go.
